claims.text: In situ heating aberration-corrected TEM can reveal atomic-scale structural changes in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles at high temperatures.
The observed structural changes will correlate with predicted enhanced thermal stability arising from thermodynamic contributions.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a near-equiatomic composition.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles exhibit a homogeneous, single-phase structure at room temperature.
A TEM heating stage can provide a controlled high-temperature environment that mimics service conditions.
In situ heating AC-TEM can monitor lattice distortions, atomic rearrangements, segregation, and phase transformations in real time at atomic scale.
Heating produces thermodynamic driving forces that enable atomic diffusion and structural reordering.
Thermally driven diffusion and reordering should produce observable changes in interatomic spacing or local phase transformations.
Modulations in interatomic spacing and local phase transformations would confirm theoretical predictions of enhanced thermal stability.
Shifts in lattice parameters or formation of secondary phases during heating would constitute direct evidence of thermodynamic contributions to thermal stability.
High-entropy nanoparticles are theoretically predicted to possess enhanced thermal stability based on thermodynamic arguments.
Very slow or subtle diffusion processes may be unresolved because of the spatial and temporal resolution limits of in situ heating AC-TEM.
Electron-beam exposure can produce effects that must be distinguished from thermally driven structural changes.
Local heterogeneity and measurement limitations make it uncertain whether atomic-scale observations can be quantitatively correlated with bulk thermal stability.
High-resolution TEM images and electron diffraction patterns can detect temperature-dependent atomic, crystal-structure, and phase-composition changes.
Failure to observe significant temperature-correlated structural changes would falsify the proposed enhanced-thermal-stability hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis concerns enhanced thermal stability, but phase transformations and secondary-phase formation are treated as confirming evidence, while an absence of structural change is designated as falsification. Structural retention during heating would ordinarily be the direct observation expected from thermal stability, so the proposed evidentiary direction is internally reversed.

The initial material is asserted to be homogeneous and single phase, yet formation of secondary phases is presented as evidence supporting enhanced stability rather than as possible evidence of destabilization; no retention criterion is given.
